newsitem.title: USA: Platinum demand in US auto catalysts flat at best.
newsitem.headline: Platinum demand in US auto catalysts flat at best.

text.p: The use of platinum in auto catalysts to scrub emissions will flatten and even decline this year in the United States, but any loss will be partly compensated by rising car production elsewhere in the Americas, Johnson Matthey said.
North America consumed 790,000 ounces of platinum in auto catalysts last year.
"I think 1997 could be flat to slightly down," Johnson Matthey's market research manager for North America, Ellen Zadoff, said.
"We will probably see this going forward. Platinum is doing exactly what we expected it to do."
Monday, Johnson Matthey, a refiner and fabricator of platinum group metals, published its Platinum 1997 report.
Globally, auto catalysts consumed 1.8 million ounces of platinum and 2.3 million ounces of palladium last year, accounting for 33 percent and 37 percent of their respective total demand.

The lack of growth in the U.S. auto sector for platinum is due to Ford's decision to introduce palladium only catalysts in more and more vehicles to meet low emission targets in certain key states such as California, Zadoff said.
Other car makers are also using more palladium and less platinum and rhodium in order to meet emission targets, but shy away from relying too much on one metal, Zadoff said.
The use of palladium in North American catalysts has risen sharply, from 950,000 ounces in 1995 to 1.23 million in 1996 as a result of Ford's policy.
"Even though you are seeing palladium taking a strong jump, you are not seeing a dramatic drop in platinum and rhodium," Zadoff said.
Much will depend on how quickly low emission cars are introduced in all the 49 contiguous states. At present they run on roads in California, New York and Massachusetts.
Latin American platinum group metal prospects in catalysts were good, especially in Mexico whose car production rebounded after a bad 1995.
But with no new emissions legislation, Mexican PGM consumption is expected to remain flat this year.
Nevertheless, inspections in Mexico to check if cars conform to current emission standards are becoming more stringent, and this may help white metal consumption.
Most of Mexico's car production in the next few years will be destined for the U.S. market, thereby boosting palladium consumption in particular, Zadoff said.
Economic recoveries in Brazil and Argentina also bode well for white metal demand.
Argentinian legislation in effect from this year will ensure all new vehicles are equipped with catalysts, along with any exported to Paraguay and Uruguay due to Mercosur rules.
Brazil also ruled this year that all cars must have catalysts.
"Therefore overall, a very healthy jump in PGMs for South America," Zadoff said. "This could take some of the pressure off (platinum in) the U.S."

And the growth of diesel autos in Europe from 22 percent of total vehicle sales last year to 28 percent by 2000 will bolster platinum, the key component of catalysts in diesel-driven vehicles with no talk of substitution by palladium, Zadoff said.
